opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a straight line. I came to Oxford with a math background, and I think I arrived with this slightly naive idea that the brain would be a beautiful, clean system waiting for the right equations. What I found was that it's incredibly messy. You'd be in a lab or reading papers, and there's this enormous amount of experimental detail: recordings from neurons, behavioral data, anatomy. It was overwhelming, and it was also exciting.

The turning point for me was realizing that the questions I cared most about weren't really "what does this particular neuron do," but "what is the brain *computing*, and why does it compute it that way?" Once you frame it like that, you naturally reach for mathematical and computational tools. How does a network of noisy, unreliable units end up doing something as robust as learning, or memory, or reasoning? That's a question about algorithms and representations as much as biology.

There was also something very satisfying about being a mathematician in a room full of experimentalists. You realize the theory side isn't just decoration. A good model can tell you which experiment is actually worth running. That back-and-forth, using math to make sense of messy data and then having the data push back on your elegant assumptions, is what drew me in.

Looking back, I think that period also planted a seed for what I care about now. Studying how the brain learns and reasons made me think a lot about what reasoning *is*, and whether we can build systems that do it in a rigorous, verifiable way. Neuroscience taught me humility about intelligence, but it also made me really curious about whether we could engineer some of it ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response attributes her shift to questions about computation, mathematical tools, and theory meeting experiments. It does not identify killing a mouse as part of Oxford’s animal-experimentation licensing process.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I went to Oxford, I actually came in thinking I would study neuroscience in the classic experimental sense. I was fascinated by the brain as an object, by how something made of cells and electrical signals could produce memory, language, mathematical reasoning. I spent time in the lab, I did the wet work, I looked at recordings, and I loved it.

But fairly quickly I ran into a frustration that I think a lot of people in the field feel. You collect this enormous amount of data, and then you stare at it and realize the bottleneck is not the data anymore. The bottleneck is having a framework that explains what the data means. You can record from thousands of neurons and still not be able to say, in a precise way, what computation those neurons are doing. That gap between observation and explanation really bothered me.

And I had always loved mathematics. At Oxford I kept gravitating toward the more theoretical courses, dynamical systems, information theory, probability, and at some point it clicked that these were the tools that could actually close that gap. Computational neuroscience was the place where you could say, here is a model, here is what it predicts, and here is how we test it against the brain. It turned a descriptive science into something closer to physics, where you can make quantitative claims and be wrong in an informative way.

So I would say it was less a sharp turn and more a gradual realization that the questions I cared about, how does a system learn, how does it generalize, how does it represent structure, were fundamentally mathematical questions wearing biological clothing. Once I saw it that way, moving toward the computational side felt inevitable. And honestly, that same way of thinking carried straight into what I do now with AI and reasoning systems. The brain was my first example of an intelligent system I desperately wanted to understand, and the tools I picked up trying to understand it are the ones I still use every day.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes the shift to frustration with interpreting experimental data and a growing interest in mathematical tools. It does not mention killing a mouse or Oxford’s animal-experimentation licensing process.

astra-6.text: Studying the brain at Oxford drew me toward the gap between observing something and explaining it. You can describe what neurons do, but how does that activity give rise to learning or decision-making? I was interested in how mathematical models could make those questions more precise. That’s what drew me toward computational neuroscience: the possibility of turning an intuition about how the brain works into a model you can test.

sol-6.1.text: Studying the brain made me interested in how we move from describing what we observe to explaining how it works. Computational neuroscience appealed to me because it offered a way to make ideas precise: build a model, ask what it predicts, and compare that with the evidence. That connection between understanding the brain and thinking mathematically was what drew me toward it.
